record.paper_title: Neutrino-nucleus interactions: open questions and future projects
record.context_brief: Low-energy beta-beam sensitivity to neutrino magnetic moment
record.original_question: Can a low-energy beta-beam source at rest, combined with very low-threshold detectors and accurately calculated neutrino fluxes, improve current direct limits on the neutrino magnetic moment by almost an order of magnitude, and what precise sensitivity remains after detailed detector-response simulation?

evidence.quote: To improve present direct limits on the neutrino magnetic moment one needs : i) very intense neutrino sources of well-known fluxes; ii) very low threshold detectors.
Clearly in this case - as for a static source [45,46,47] - the neutrino fluxes can be very accurately calculated.
This indicates that the present direct limits might be improved by almost an order of magnitude, the precise value requiring a detailed simulation of the detector response.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a hypothetical neutrino source consisting of radioactive ions decaying at rest, which produces a pure flavor neutrino flux (a "beta-beam at rest") whose energy spectrum is determined by the known beta-decay kinematics of the parent isotope and can therefore be computed with high precision. Suppose this source is coupled to a detector with a very low recoil-energy threshold (well below 1 keV scale), so that elastic neutrino–electron (and/or neutrino–nucleus) scattering events at small energy transfer can be recorded. The differential cross section for such scattering receives a Standard Model weak contribution plus an additional contribution proportional to the square of the neutrino magnetic moment μ_ν (in units of the Bohr magneton μ_B), the latter being strongly enhanced as the recoil energy tends to zero.

Question: Determine whether such a configuration can improve the current direct experimental upper limits on the neutrino magnetic moment μ_ν by close to an order of magnitude, and compute the precise sensitivity on μ_ν (in units of μ_B) that remains achievable after a detailed simulation of the detector response, including realistic energy resolution, threshold effects, and background subtraction.
artifact.status_search_result: Feasibility studies indicate that a low-energy beta-beam source combined with low-threshold detectors could in principle probe neutrino magnetic moments at the level of a few × 10⁻¹¹ μ_B, comparable to or slightly better than current direct limits, but this requires very high ion production rates (≳ 10¹⁵ s⁻¹) and no such facility has been realized. Current best direct laboratory limits on μ_ν come from reactor and dark-matter direct-detection experiments (e.g., CONUS, XENONnT), with the precise achievable beta-beam sensitivity depending on detector-response simulations that have not been definitively settled. The status of the specific claim of nearly an order-of-magnitude improvement therefore remains unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Prospects for Detecting a Neutrino Magnetic Moment with a Tritium Source and Beta-beams
status_evidence.snippet: Low-energy beta-beams with sufficiently rapid production of ions could improve the limits on the neutrino magnetic moment to the level of a few × 10⁻¹¹ μ_B, requiring ion production ≥ 10¹⁵ s⁻¹.
status_evidence.claim: Beta-beam sensitivities of order 10⁻¹¹ μ_B are projected but contingent on demanding source intensities.

status_evidence.title: First upper limits on neutrino electromagnetic properties from CONUS
status_evidence.snippet: CONUS sets upper limits on neutrino electromagnetic properties from coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering at a reactor.
status_evidence.claim: Current direct limits on μ_ν continue to be set by reactor and direct-detection experiments, not beta-beams.

status_evidence.title: PDG 2025: Neutrino properties listings
status_evidence.snippet: Particle Data Group compilation of current direct limits on neutrino magnetic moments.
status_evidence.claim: No beta-beam-based limit on μ_ν has superseded existing direct limits as of 2025.
